performers: Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau, baritone; Berlin Philharmonic; Rudolf Kempe, conductor
intro: “Nun will die Sonn’ so hell aufgeh’n” is the first of the Kindertotenlieder, a song in which the sun rises after a child’s death. Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau sings it with the Berlin Philharmonic under Rudolf Kempe. An oboe and a horn play the opening alone.

sections.label: A · Oboe and horn introduction
sections.mNote: Oboe and horn play two lines before the baritone enters.

sections.label: A′ · The sun shines for everyone
sections.mNote: Flute and bassoon join the returning phrases.

sections.label: B · Horns take the vocal melody
sections.mNote: The horns take over the vocal melody; the violins rise.

sections.label: A″ · A lamp goes out: reprise
sections.mNote: Oboe and flute play the opening material again

cues.title: Oboe and horn duet
cues.text: The oboe rises by small steps while a horn plays below it, and the strings rest. Mahler marks the music Langsam und schwermütig; nicht schleppend, slow and melancholy, without dragging. Fischer-Dieskau sings the first line, about the rising sun, over this wind duet.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, p. 3: Langsam und schwermütig; nicht schleppend. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Deaths of Rückert’s children
cues.text: Friedrich Rückert’s children Luise and Ernst died on 31 December 1833 and 16 January 1834. In his grief he wrote more than four hundred poems, none of them meant for print. Mahler later chose five of them.
cues.evidence: Reinhold Kubik, Universal Edition introduction to Kindertotenlieder (autumn 2008), gives the two dates and the 400-odd poems, published after Rückert’s death: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Kindertotenlieder/P0045027. The Mahler Foundation counts 428 poems and says they were not intended for publication: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/kindertotenlieder/kindertotenlieder-introduction/

cues.title: Second couplet, return of opening
cues.text: The second couplet of Rückert’s poem reads “Das Unglück geschah nur mir allein” (the disaster happened to me alone). The opening tune returns. The flute plays above the voice, and the bassoon repeats its small upward steps.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 6–8, second couplet of Rückert’s poem; our translation. Geert Woltjer discusses the flute doubling and bassoon figure: https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler1.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Third couplet
cues.text: The third couplet is addressed to the father himself, who must sink his night into eternal light. Horns take up the earlier vocal melody and the voice enters with a new line. After the words end, the violins continue the rising line.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 9–14. The third couplet and the exchange of oboe, horn and vocal phrases are discussed at https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler1.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Footnote in the full score, 1905
cues.text: A footnote on the first page of the score asks that the five songs be treated as one inseparable whole. Mahler added that their continuity was to be kept even against the applause that would normally follow a “number”.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460 (1905), printed p. 3, footnote: “Diese 5 Gesänge sind als ein einheitliches, untrennbares Ganzes gedacht …”; our translation. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 The same instruction is printed on the title page of the 1905 vocal score: https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/KtL/KtLprints.htm

cues.title: Return of the opening melody
cues.text: At “Ein Lämplein verlosch in meinem Zelt” (a little lamp went out in my tent), Fischer-Dieskau returns to the opening melody. Oboe and flute bring back their short phrases, and the glockenspiel sounds in the gaps between them.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 14–17, Rückert’s final couplet; our translation. Page 14 marks the orchestral return zurückkehrend.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Vienna, 1905
cues.text: On 29 January 1905 Mahler conducted the first performance of the cycle in the Kleiner Musikvereinssaal in Vienna, with Friedrich Weidemann as soloist. The concert sold out days beforehand, and tickets for the afternoon dress rehearsal were put on sale. A repeat followed on 3 February.
cues.evidence: Paul Banks, The Music of Gustav Mahler: A Catalogue of Manuscript and Printed Sources, Kindertotenlieder: chronology (29 January and 3 February 1905, Kleine Saal des Musikvereins, concert of the Vereinigung schaffender Tonkünstler Wiens) and the first-performance note (sold out by 24 January, dress-rehearsal tickets released, repeat arranged): https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/KtL/KtL.htm

cues.title: Closing bars, harp and glockenspiel
cues.text: The baritone’s final word is “Welt” (world). The harp continues its rocking figure, with soft glockenspiel notes above it. Mahler leaves the last bar empty under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 17: final vocal phrase, harp, glockenspiel and the closing bar of rests with fermatas. The existing cue marks the closing passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The oboe returns for the second couplet
transitions.to: A′ · The sun shines for everyone
transitions.how: The oboe returns over the harp’s rocking D-minor figure and the glockenspiel notes, which continue. The introduction to the second couplet is shorter than the first. The flute joins the vocal line and the bassoon takes the repeated C♯–D steps below. The singer’s rhythm changes so that the stress falls on “mir” (me).
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 6–8; Woltjer, song I, discussion of bars 22 onwards. https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler1.html

transitions.title: The horn takes over the vocal tune
transitions.from: A′ · The sun shines for everyone
transitions.to: B · Horns take the vocal melody
transitions.how: After “allgemein”, the horn extends the closing phrase over low notes in the clarinet and bassoon. The oboe follows with a more urgent phrase. In the next passage the horn plays the first vocal melody while the voice sings a countermelody against it. D minor and D major alternate as the text turns towards eternal light.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 9–13; Woltjer, song I, discussion of bars 36–59. https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler1.html

transitions.title: Flute and oboe find home
transitions.from: B · Horns take the vocal melody
transitions.to: A″ · A lamp goes out: reprise
transitions.how: Marked zurückkehrend — returning — the flute’s running notes soften around the oboe’s opening phrase. Horns hold below; glockenspiel notes punctuate the retreat. The strings fall silent before the last couplet restores the D-minor vocal melody.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 14–15, zurückkehrend and the final couplet. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425

source.title: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, full score (C. F. Kahnt, plate 4460)
source.locator: Song I, printed pp. 3–17: oboe and horn introduction, muted strings, the violins’ rising phrases and the final harp and glockenspiel.

timeline.note: Opening duet, oboe above the first horn; voice and strings silent.
Harp and muted violas and cellos accompany the baritone’s first stanza.
The oboe’s opening phrase returns as the father names the loss that belongs to him alone.
The first violins enter with a high melody as the text turns to eternal light.
Flute and oboe bring back the opening phrases before the last stanza.
Harp and strings accompany the father’s blessing of the world’s joyful light.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor.
